speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: GENEVA CONFERENCE
subsubtopic: STATEMENT TO BE MADE BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will have noticed that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) is in his seat this afternoon. He returned to Ottawa late last night after what I understand was a long and rather fatiguing air journey, and he will be reporting to his colleagues at two o'clock tomorrow afternoon. We had hoped there might be a very early occasion arranged for reporting to the house at a time when the house would not have to be content with his report on what had taken place, but would have an opportunity of asking questions and discussing the matters involved in that report.
Thursday and Friday are to be devoted to the consideration of the estimates and we had hoped that the committee on external affairs would have made its report and that these estimates could be called on Thursday to
provide an opportunity, in accordance with the rule, both for the report and for questions and discussion.
However, it has been found that Thursday would not suit the convenience of some hon. members who would be very much interested in the proceedings, and I would therefore suggest that we do that on Friday, and that as soon as the estimates are reported by the committee on external affairs they be referred back to the committee of the whole and called for consideration on Friday, when the minister would report on what took place while he was away at Geneva, and when there would be an opportunity for questions to be asked of the minister and for hon. members to take part in any discussion that might naturally flow from that report, and from the questions and answers.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO RAISING OF MARKET QUOTAS IN WEST

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO RAISING OF MARKET QUOTAS IN WEST
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Is he in a position to say now what are the prospects of the market quotas for wheat being generally raised throughout the western provinces in order to provide additional cash for the farmers at this time of year?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO RAISING OF MARKET QUOTAS IN WEST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is possible at this time to speed up deliveries from the country. I am told that the outstanding orders for the forwarding of grain will take care of all points that have not as yet reached the five-bushel quota. Over and above the five-bushel quota, considerable progress is being made in bringing all points up to the seven-bushel quota. We believe that situation can be achieved in due course.
The difficulty is that we have a great preponderance of No. 2 northern wheat and there is a limit to the extent that we can block up our facilities in the east by filling them with No. 2 northern wheat. However, we now have a sufficient movement of No. 2 northern wheat to enable us to clean up the five-bushel quota points. I point out to hon. members that the specified acreage is about 70 million acres. On a seven-bushel quota that in itself will amount to a delivery of about 500 million bushels. The special quotas deliverable to coarse grains and for other purposes will raise that amount by at least another 50 million bushels. Hence after we reach the seven-bushel quota we shall be working on total deliveries of over 550 million bushels whereas the average deliveries over the past ten years have been about 510 million bushels.

However, I can quite appreciate that this house can dispose of the question without consideration by the royal commission, and since the minister has elected to do so I should like to say a few words about the bill.
Inventions by Public Servants
While it may be easy for some officials to understand, the house as a whole might not be so well informed as to the implications of the provisions of this bill. We are dealing with a patent which is a reward given to an inventor for having disclosed his invention to the public. In the ordinary course of events, Mr. Speaker, a patent is granted freely to any inventor in this country, provided he is the first inventor and makes a sufficient and proper disclosure. In the ordinary course of master and servant, the problems are not too difficult. The invention belongs to the servant, whether or not he has invented something on the time of the master, whether or not he has done so with the machines or tools of the master. The only thing the master usually gets, unless there is a specific contract, is an equity in the invention or the use of the invention for his own purposes, depending on the specific contract, and some benefits from the invention.
The relationship we are considering today, however, is that of the crown and crown employees. This makes the situation more difficult. As between an ordinary person and the crown, the crown can use the invention subject only to such award as might be made by the commissioner of patents. Now, the crown wishes to establish a proper relationship between the crown and the inventor who is a public servant, and that makes the situation quite complicated. The complication arises in view of the fact that the whole system of patents is based on the reward to an inventor for making his disclosure to the public, and because the intention of this bill is to put the servant of the crown, not in an inferior position but in a different position from that of the ordinary servant in relation to his master.
As I stated before, we are interested here in the relationship between the crown and its employees. The distinction being made in this bill, and an important one, is to define what inventions shall belong to the crown and what inventions shall not. The definition, therefore, that may be given in the bill will be of great importance. I quite appreciate that the purpose of this bill, generally speaking, is to cover certain specific cases in which inventors, who are servants of the crown, made inventions while they were employees of the crown and have not acknowledged their inventions to the departmental minister. The provisions of this bill should not be made so strict as to discourage civil servants from giving of their best, so that the public at large may get the benefit.

Inventions by Public Servants
The provisions in our act now are rather stringent. Broadly speaking, we have a provision in the Patent Act, that is section 47, which states:
Every patent granted in respect of an invention made by a person while employed in the public service of Canada, and relating to the nature of his employment is . . . subject to the following conditions:
Generally speaking, the conditions are that the crown is declared to have an interest, and that any royalties derived from the said patent will be divided between the servant and the crown. There is another important provision which may not appear in this bill, covered by subsection 4 of section 47, which says:
Nothing herein contained shall be construed to restrict the right of the inventor to the full enjoyment of his invention outside of Canada.
Now, that is the general situation of an inventor who is a servant of the crown. There is also, however, the National Defence Act, Atomic Energy Control Act and the Research Council Act, which specifically cover the employees of these departments, and which contain stringent regulations. I believe that is understandable because these employees, by their duties, are inventors for the crown. Those acts specifically state that any invention by employees working under those acts belongs to the crown. I thought I should mention those facts in order to illustrate that this situation is not new.
There are broad provisions in the Patent Act covering civil servants, and specific provisions in the other acts covering servants of the crown who are research men. The point now, then, is to find out what is the appropriate course to follow. As I understand it, the government would like to have more uniform legislation on the subject. As I said before, however, the rights and benefits accruing to public servants should not be fettered or reduced so as to discourage them from making further inventions in the public interest. The most important element is that any invention that is not of a type relating to the employment of the civil servant should not be restricted by this bill. This bill should set forth in absolute terms the inventions to which the crown shall have an absolute right, but I am hoping that this definition will release all public servants who are not, by the nature of their employment, directed towards improving and devising new methods, articles or processes. That is the most important part. As I said before, I have no quarrel with restrictions being imposed on people who, from the nature of their employment, are research men.


The second important part, no doubt, is the protection of the rights of any public servant against delays by the minister in deciding whether an invention is or is not of a class which the crown claims to own. An inventor, whoever he may be, should have the right to apply for his patent in Canada. He probably would not go to the expense of doing so if he thought the patent should belong to the crown. But, in any event, any delay in filing an application would be prejudicial in establishing prior conception rights and protecting treaty rights involved in the invention, whether to the crown or to the public servant himself.
I have already mentioned to the minister that the inventor, who is a civil servant, a public servant, might not be restrained from filing an application as soon as he desires.
Another point involved in a patent matter of course is the use of the invention abroad. It is doubtful if the ordinary gratuity which would be granted a civil servant would really cover the value of his invention for use abroad; and in this case under the present bill as I understand it the crown would have the right to the invention the world over. That is understandable. But I wish to point out that it would be hardly fair for the crown to hold the right to inventions universally and not to exercise its right to take out patents in other countries without giving the opportunity within the required time to the inventor to do so.
Perhaps hon. members know that most countries require that application be filed in another country within one year of the filing date in Canada. So if the crown elects not to file the application outside of Canada after the year, we would simply be giving the benefit of the invention to other countries for nothing, whereas we probably would be in a position to charge royalties to our own people within this country. I am sure the minister will bear this point in mind.
I do not wish to deal in detail with the matter of compensation. Under the present statute, in the Patent Act, the right of the ordinary public servant is preserved. There has been no complaint about that and, I believe, there have been no serious difficulties. The public servant is entitled to share his royalty with the crown in accordance with the decision of the commissioner of patents.
I do not know what benefits have accrued to inventors under the other statutes-the National Defence Act, the Research Council Act and the Atomic Energy Control Act.
These matters have not been made public, and I do not know how satisfied or dissatisfied employees are. But apparently they must

be satisfied because there has been no mention, at least publicly, of their dissatisfaction. In any event, there is also the fact that people who are not affected by those acts seem to have been satisfied by the supervisory provisions of the Patent Act, as set out under section 46.
These, therefore, are the general problems involved in the bill. The other acts which deal with other departments are well directed, and it is difficult to associate inventions of ordinary inventors with inventors who are of the research type. I wish the house to bear in mind that under a bill of this kind a cleaner or a stenographer, a physicist or a medical doctor would all be treated in the same way. They would all have to submit their inventions to their ministers, of whatever nature such inventions might be, before filing application. And such filing could not be made without the consent of the minister.
That is why I stated in the beginning that any delay caused by the decision of the minister might have serious consequences for the inventor who invented something of a type which the crown should not hold.
Another point that should be kept in mind is that if the provisions of this bill are carried through, necessarily there will have to be an organization to carry out the provisions properly. It cannot be done haphazardly. There should be a central authority to decide which patents are of a type belonging to the crown. Such authority should decide the type of invention which must be retained by the crown or given back to the inventor. That same authority should decide what gratuity there should be, and also should take appropriate action through a patent solicitor to patent the invention either in Canada or throughout the world, and also to defend lawsuits or to take lawsuits or legal action, wherever necessary. That is, in effect, putting ourselves in the patent business.
While I do not wish to deal with this question in detail, it does bring up a very tricky subject. There are definite facts and opinions on both sides as to whether the crown, once it has expended public money on research, should hold a patent and collect royalties from those who exploit the patent for commerce, or whether it should simply give the benefit freely to the people, and let the inventor have his benefits outside, if he can.
As I said before, I do not wish to take the time to discuss that problem at length. Just the same, however, it does involve the question as to whether the crown, as such, should go into the business of holding, maintaining and licensing patents. Obviously it is done 83276-317*
Inventions by Public Servants under the Research Council Act. Probably it can operate in certain circumstances. And since the matter is not involved here I will not discuss it further.
However, if this bid is to be implemented properly, then a proper organization should be established. At present the departments apply through different solicitors for their own patents. They have different methods of doing it. It might be that, in the opinion of those who are looking forward to proper development, the patent office in time should have a staff equipped to settle all these problems, and that the commissioner of patents, as he does under the old act, should have to settle what inventions belong to the crown, what gratuity should be allowed, and say who should apply for patents in the right of the crown. These of course are matters for regulation and are not matters known to those who are discussing the bill.
In conclusion I have only one further point to make. As I said earlier, I do not know how employees of the government feel about this bill. I have no reason to believe that they are not satisfied; I have no way of knowing that. However, 1 do appreciate the desirability of protecting the interests of the crown in respect of inventions which are directly connected with the kind of employment carried on by public servants. At the same time I am interested in protecting the ordinary individual who, while employed by the crown, develops an invention which is not of that type. I am also interested in servants of the crown who have invented new processes or new articles of manufacture or new compositions of matters which are related to their employment. I should like to see them get a proper gratuity. That is another important point.
If I have searched too deeply I apologize to the house; but since this subject matter is germane to my usual calling I thought I should bring those matters to the attention of the house. I have no doubt that the minister will appreciate that in doing so I am trying to assist him.

I must say that when I heard his remarks on that subject I was tremendously impressed by the fact that every government has a great responsibility, not only to assure that inventions which may be the result of research work either by government employees or by military, naval or air experts should become the property of the crown, under fair conditions and terms, but also that there should be some protection against the possibility of what occurred in that particular case.
As the right hon. gentleman has every reason to know, there was some surprise that toward the end of the war there were Heinkel and Messerschmitt aircraft operating with jet engines of comparable quality, or perhaps in some cases even better quality than the British machines which had been developed from the original British patent.
This is no reflection upon the inventor. It certainly is no reflection on the loyalty and good faith of those sorely pressed and extremely conscientious men who did not see the possibilities of that new invention. It is not very often that a Whittle invents a jet engine or a Watson-Watt invents radar. Nevertheless these things do occur.
I wonder if this is not something that should be under wider discretion than the discretion of a single minister in whose department such inventions might arise. The right hon. gentleman and I have not always agreed on every detail of matters that have come up in the house, but I do recognize his very wide contact with inventions and the handling of these inventions, and I know how readily he will admit that it is difficult to judge in advance the full possibilities of some invention which, at the moment, might seem to be of a radical character, such as the jet engine was at the time it came forward.
Men whose minds were engaged with the immediate problem of defence and the immediate problem of getting engine production felt that this was such a wide departure from the ordinary propellor-driven engine

There was reluctance to provide the additional metal necessary for these new experiments. In some way, the danger of this becoming available to the enemy perhaps was not fully recognized. Perhaps it was that they simply did not regard this as anything more than a wildly imaginary device. In any event, the fact remains the patent was applied for. subtopic: PROVISION FOR OWNERSHIP, MANAGEMENT AND PAYMENT
speechtext:
This is the section which gives to the governor in council power to make regulations which would include, amongst other things-as has been pointed out-the prescribing of the kind and methods of granting awards, and so on; and it also includes a very important category, as the section stands now, of regulations prescribing rules of practice and procedure respecting any appeal or application under this act to the exchequer court. By an earlier section I suggest that if a public servant questions whether his invention was made within the scope of his employment so as to be within the purview of this act, with the result that the patent to it and the rights to it are vested in the crown, it is a question for the minister to decide. In other words, the minister decides whether it is one of those inventions or not. If the minister gives a decision that is adverse to the public servant, then his only recourse is to appeal to the exchequer court and to try to convince that court that this was an invention made by him in his


own time and not so necessarily related to his employment as automatically to fall within the scope of this act.
That may be a highly important question and may involve considerable financial stakes for the public servant. I should think it would be most likely and most probable that he would go to see a lawyer and that his appeal would be taken to the exchequer court in that way. He would probably go to see patent attorneys and other lawyers as well. What I question here is the desirability of giving to the governor in council the right to make the rules or, as the wording is here, the right to make regulations prescribing rules of practice and procedure respecting any appeal or application under this act to the exchequer court.
There are several grounds on which I question the advisability of that provision. Putting it on its lowest possible plane, the first one is that the governor in council, desiring to discourage servants from appealing, might make regulations as to security for costs and things of that nature which would in effect prohibit the public servant from appealing and in effect take away altogether the right of appeal. I admit that that is putting it at its lowest level, but I am looking at all the possibilities. It may just be possible that government policy at some future time would harden against inventors having any rights to these things and there would be the temptation and the inclination to raise the amount required as security for costs.
In the second place, not even the Patent Act itself confers this right, namely the right of the governor in council to make regulations respecting practice and procedure on appeal to the exchequer court, even with respect to sections 67 to 72 of that act which are the sections of the Patent Act now covering the cases of inventions by public servants. There the appeal is to the exchequer court if the public servant and the commissioner of patents disagree; but the appeal is under the ordinary rules of court, as is the case with every other appeal. The governor in council has absolutely no right to lay down the rules with respect to an appeal.
Finally, as a matter of general practice I suggest that since the exchequer court is given the right-as is every other court-to make its own rules prescribing the practice and procedures in that court, whether it be a motion of first instance or an appeal from another court, it is not necessary to give to the governor in council the power to make rules in this case. Furthermore, I submit that it is undesirable and it is a wrong prin*-ciple to give the governor in council power

to make these rules. It the exchequer court did not have the right to make rules governing procedure on appeals in matters of this kind, such a provision might be necessary; but it now has that power. If this subsection were to carry and were to be included, the result would be that a legal practitioner, in addition to having to look at the rules of court in order to find out the rules applicable to this appeal, would have to go and to search through the orders in council and look in the Canada Gazette to see whether just the other day the governor in council had happened to pass another order in council affecting these rules.
Any member of the committee who is a lawyer will, I am quite sure, agree with me when I say that it is difficult enough now to keep track of the rules of court and that it is not appropriate that, in addition to looking at the rules of court and searching them to make certain that he has the latest amendments, the practitioner should also have to search through the Canada Gazette to see whether the governor in council happened lately to have passed any amendments to the rules governing the practice and procedure on this particular type of appeal. Because I submit that this provision is neither necessary nor in accordance with sound principles I move:
That clause 12 be amended by deleting from subsection (a) the following words:
(iii) any appeal or application under this act to the exchequer court.

I submit to the minister, with respect, that he is not correct in his interpretation of the effect of paragraph (iii). In my submission the right to make regulations with regard to the rules of practice and procedure respecting appeals to the exchequer court is not necessarily inherent in the right to make regulations for carrying out the purposes and provisions of the act. When you give the governor general in council the power to make regulations for carrying out the purposes and provisions of the act it would, I submit, not be held by a court that the right to make regulations prescribing rules of practice and procedure on appeal was necessarily inherent in that power. An appeal is something quite outside of and apart from this act or the carrying into force of this act. This section is very clear. It actually gives the governor in council the power to differentiate between the right of appeal of the civil servant to the Exchequer Court of Canada and the right of the ordinary citizen of the country. Surely we do not want to incorporate in the law a principle whereby every other citizen in Canada shall have certain rights and shall follow certain regulations when appealing to the exchequer court but those regulations shall not apply to civil servants. The minister says that he hazards the guess that the reason is the one given. Certainly we should not depart from the ordinary principle that everyone is equal before the law and by this provision allow the civil servant to be placed in a lower category than every other citizen in the country.
As a matter of fact, under the present provision the governor in council by order in council could simply place a roadblock in the way of the civil servant wishing to appeal to the exchequer court. In one section the right is provided for, but under the regulations the civil servant should be presumed to be in the same position as every other person, namely, that he should be required to put up certain determined security as the basis for appeal. This section permits the governor in council to make a provision


whereby a dangerous immunity from judicial supervision will be granted in so far as civil servants are concerned.
I suggest that we do not wish to set up two types of citizens with respect to right of appeal to the courts, the first being the majority of the Canadian people and the second being civil servants who would be granted lesser rights than those granted to others. I am sure that the other provisions regarding regulations are simply those necessary for the carrying out of the provisions of the act. The section reads:

(a) prescribing rules of practice and procedure respecting
(i) applications for patents pursuant to this act-

- (ii) the determination of questions whether an invention is vested in Her Majesty by this act-

The intervention of the hon. member for Prince Albert has, I think, somewhat cleared my own mind. He says that we do not want to make one law for public servants and another law for other citizens. Mr. Chairman, perhaps hon. members would welcome a brief statement as to the purpose of the resolution. As the resolution indicates, the purpose of this bill is to prescribe the pension provisions for and the manner in which those pension provisions are to apply to persons transferring from the public

service to certain crown corporations. It is designed to bring consistency with the new Public Service Superannuation Act and will provide that these transferred employees will become members of the pension plan of the corporations to which they will be transferred.
I should add however that the Public Service Superannuation Act made provision for the entry into reciprocal transfer agreements between the government of Canada and crown corporations to cover the transferability of pension rights when a contributor under that act transferred his employment to that of a crown corporation or vice versa. Thus where these agreements are concluded a transferred employee may obtain full credit for his prior service under the pension plan of his new employer.
Because of its close relation with the Public Service Superannuation Act it is intended that this new act will have effect from January 1, 1954, the day on which the Public Service Superannuation Act came into force.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say only a few words. The object of the bill to be based on this resolution seems to be a commendable one, and one which I believe will meet with general support in the House of Commons.
My main reason for rising is to suggest that the principle underlying this legislation is so important and so commendable that in my view it should be extended to apply on a much wider basis. I believe this is not the first instance of mobility of pension rights being established, and I suggest this move is greatly needed. This is a subject about which my colleague the hon. member for Cape Breton South has spoken frequently; and it seems to me some thinking should be given to establishing a master plan or broadening the Government Annuities Act, or finding some other means to make it possible for people to move from the public service to crown corporations, or from either of those categories of employment into private industry, or to move from one private industry to another, or from private industry into the public service, while at the same time carrying with them their pension rights. In this way, upon reaching pensionable age they would retain such rights as they had earned across their working years.
Undoubtedly great progress has been made in the concept of retirement pensions. Many more pension plans are in effect today; many more people are covered by such plans than was the case ten or twenty years ago, and this is all to the good. But there are many instances where pension plans freeze employees to certain jobs. After they have been
Crown Corporations
on those jobs for a few years their rights are such that it makes it difficult for them to consider moving to other jobs, lest they sacrifice such rights as they have gained. Similarly there are areas of employment denied to people because they have passed a certain age, and an employer may not want to take in someone who has passed that age, when he has no pension rights to bring with him or no way in which he could transfer such rights.
In both those cases the situation would be improved greatly if, as I have indicated, there was greater mobility of pension rights. We support the principle set out in the resolution upon which the bill will be based. If I have any quarrel with this measure, it is that it is so limited in its scope.
My further quarrel with the government is that though this idea has been spoken of around here on many occasions, not only on the opposition side of the house but on the government side as well, so little seems to have been done to establish the mobility of pension rights for all our people, whether they are in public service or in crown corporations or working for one private industry or another.
Let it be very clear that we have not yet had the last word in establishing an adequate pension system for all the people of this country. Many more improvements have to be made, and one of those necessary improvements is to extend this very principle of the mobility of pension rights.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE EMPLOYMENT OF UNITED STATES PERSONNEL AND IMMIGRANTS AS RADIO OPERATORS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 446, to amend the Radio Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, section 7 of the Radio Act provides that no person shall be employed as a radio operator on any coast, land, or mobile station unless he is a British subject, and the section goes on to make certain exceptions to this provision.
It has become necessary, by virtue of agreement with the United States for certain operations to take place in Canada by United States' citizens on defence and radar stations, to exempt the operators of radio stations from the provisions of that section. At present the position is, as I previously explained, that none other than British subjects can operate these stations and it is proposed by means of this bill to cover three cases of exceptions.
First, certain aircraft pilots who by virtue of the agreements under the international civil aviation organization may operate in our country. He may fly his plane in our country but there is no point in his doing so if he cannot operate the radio, and in the case of many citizens who are not British subjects that is not possible. We therefore feel that that operation should be recognized by virtue of this amendment.
Then, with reference to the case I mentioned earlier, it was necessary by virtue of

Radio Act
the emergency powers regulations to authorize the Minister of Transport to enter into agreements with the United States government whereby United States' citizens could be exempted from the regulations laid down in section 7. That is also covered by a subsection of this bill.
Finally, there are the cases of landed immigrants who have not been in the country long enough to achieve Canadian citizenship and are not yet British subjects. Great hardship is being imposed upon many of these landed immigrants who cannot, for example, even operate a walkie-talkie in a taxi or operate a motor truck on construction jobs simply because of these regulations. The bill purports to exempt them in the performance of their duties. There is no time limit, as can be seen, such as existed in other bills which were enacted under emergency legislation and then put into various statutes of the Department of Transport. subtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE EMPLOYMENT OF UNITED STATES PERSONNEL AND IMMIGRANTS AS RADIO OPERATORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this appears to be an innocuous little bill but we believe it should be carefully scrutinized by the house before being given a second reading. The minister has given us a brief explanation of the effect of the bill, and he did the same thing on first reading. His explanation on that occasion will be found at page 4769 of Hansard for May 17, 1954 where he is reported as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the Radio Act provides that no one shall be employed as a radio operator unless he is a British subject. By virtue of the Emergency Powers Act the Minister of Transport was authorized to enter into an agreement with the United States government providing that it could establish radio stations in northern Canada and employ operators who were not British subjects. The object of this bill is to amend the Radio Act in order to implement, by way of legislation, that arrangement and also to include certain landed immigrants to be employed as radio operators and who are not yet British subjects.
Here we are proposing to hand over some Canadian keys to the United States and for that reason in particular the bill deserves extremely careful scrutiny. I would point out that under the present provisions of the Radio Act, which is chapter 233 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, there is a provision enabling the governor in council to make certain exemptions; and it seems to us to be broad enough as it reads without giving this blanket authority to let in any whole group of operators of radio stations. Section 7 of the Radio Act, in subsection 1, provides as follows:
No one shall be employed as a radio operator at any coast, land or mobile station unless he is a British subject.
fMr. Chevrier.]
I would point out that three types of stations are described, namely coast station, land station and mobile station. I would also point out that under the bill now before us authority to exempt is so broad that it covers all kinds of stations; it is not restricted to land stations. Subsection 2 of section 7 of the Radio Act provides for the taking of a declaration of secrecy. It reads in part as follows:
(2) AH radio operators at coast or land stations or on mobile stations shall take and subscribe a declaration of secrecy in the form set forth in the schedule, before a judge of any court, a notary public, a justice of the peace or a commissioner for taking affidavits,-
And so on. The next subsection of section 7 of the Radio Act makes it a crime for a person who has taken a declaration of secrecy to disclose any information. There is this firm provision for making certain that the operators have taken an oath, a declaration of secrecy, and that they can be punished severely for breaking that oath.
Then the present subsection 4 of section 7 of the Radio Act is the one which grants the power to make exemptions. As I said a few moments ago, it seems to us to be broad enough to cover the present situation. It reads as follows:
(4) The governor in council-
Which of course means the cabinet.
-may, by regulation and on such terms and conditions as he may prescribe, exempt from the operation of this section a non-resident of Canada who
(a)	is employed as a radio operator on a radio station in Canada,
(b)	holds a valid Canadian certificate of proficiency or an equivalent certificate issued by the country of which he is a citizen.-
That provision, of course, would make it broad enough to apply to an American who held an American certificate.
-and
(c)	is a resident and citizen of a country that grants a reciprocal permission to Canadian citizens to be employed as radio operators in that country.
If the United States grants a similar permission to Canadian citizens, there is in the act already power for the Canadian cabinet to grant exemption; and that seems to be the basis on which it should be kept. These rights should be reciprocal. If we are to give the Americans certain rights in our country, we should have exactly the same rights in their country. That is what is provided by subsection 4 of section 7 of the present Radio Act. If the situation now is that the Americans do not give Canadian citizens the same right, the government should get busy, negotiate with the United States and get these rights, in which event

there would be ample power under the Radio Act as it stands at the present time.
But instead of that procedure, the minister is asking for the following power. In clause (b) of the new subsection 4 there is to be given power to grant exemption-that is, the cabinet can grant exemption to:
(b) a person who is employed as a radio operator on a radio station in Canada by the government of another country or any agency thereof.
That provision just gives the blanket power to allow American operators to come into Canada. They do not even need to be employed by the United States government. They can be employed by an agency of the United States government and still get the exemption. The clause which I have just read is not confined to the United States. It states:
-a person who is employed as a radio operator on a radio station in Canada by the government of another country-
It might be any other country although, from what the minister has said, I take it that he wants this power in order to deal with American operators of these stations. However, I suggest in the first place that the power is not necessary if the United States give us the same rights that we give them. If it is necessary, I suggest that the bill should be restricted to the United States and should not be made so wide that it covers every country in the world outside of Canada. If it is to apply to the United States, then it should be set out that the power is to be exercised pursuant to an agreement between Canada and the United States. These things cannot be too carefully handled. This should be done by agreement between the two countries rather than by our just writing into our statutes a provision that people can come here from any other country-that is, a citizen of any other country-and can be exempted from our laws.
On the first reading the minister mentioned the fact that there is an agreement between Canada and the United States. We should know what that agreement is. The house should be shown that agreement. Possibly it should be made a schedule to this act. But instead of bothering to do that, the department simply brings in a bill giving blanket authority to allow operators from any other country to run these radio stations in Canada when at the same time our own Canadians running these stations are obliged to take this declaration of secrecy and are subject to these heavy penalties.
The whole Radio Act is an extremely strict one, and quite properly so. But that is all the more reason why American operators
Radio Act
should not lightly be given exemptions. I suggest that it is time the government stopped handing over blanket authority to the United States, something which in effect is being done by this bill.
Then the minister referred to the provision which is now to be written into the act to cover landed immigrants. That is a new approach. That is a new kind of legislation in Canada. At the present time the only person who can be a radio station operator in this country is one who is a British subject. Of course that includes all who are Canadian citizens. I can see that there may be cases where a new settler has come here and wants to get a job driving a taxi equipped with a radio control system. It may be that provision should be made to permit such a person to operate that type of taxi, but to do so we do not need to have an amendment which can exempt every person who is a resident of Canada from the requirements in connection with any kind of station. The amendment would cover coastal stations, land stations and mobile stations. The bill gives the government the blanket power to grant exemption to any landed immigrant.
I suggest that if a provision has to be put into the act to meet this situation the exemption should be restricted to mobile stations. We find that in section 5 of the Radio Act there is a reference to radios installed in automobiles in these words, "a radio receiving set installed in an automobile". Perhaps power should be given to exempt residents of Canada, even though they are not Canadian citizens or British subjects, in the case of a radio installed in an automobile. I do not see very much objection to a provision of that kind, but it should be restricted to the situation that has to be met today rather than providing authority for a blanket exemption.
We regard these two points, particularly the first one, as serious defects in the bill, and in the face of the objections we have raised we are hoping that the minister will go over the bill again in order to see whether or not some change cannot be made to bring the amendment much more in line with the actual situation which exists. There is one other minor point about the bill. In the new subparagraph (a) (ii) of subsection 4 we find the words:
"Holds a valid Canadian certificate of proficiency-
Then these are the words in question:
-or other authority to operate a radio station issued by the minister . . .
That looks as though the minister is seeking the power to issue some new type of certificate. I may not have read the Radio Act correctly but I cannot find out just what is meant by the words "or other authority

Radio Act
to operate a radio station issued by the minister" unless the minister is now asking for a brand new power to grant some new kind of authority for the operation of a radio station which is not already contained in the Radio Act. I place these three points before the house. I am afraid it is not quite as innocuous as it appears at first sight or as it sounded from the explanation given by the minister.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE EMPLOYMENT OF UNITED STATES PERSONNEL AND IMMIGRANTS AS RADIO OPERATORS
speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I had pointed out that if it is the wish of the government to have legislation of this kind, it is far better to achieve that end by the enacting of a statute such as this than it is to do it as it was formerly done by means of an order in council under the Emergency Powers Act. However, I should like to say just a few words with regard to the substance of the bill itself.
I am sure that no one can take issue with the desire expressed by the minister to implement the arrangements that we have under ICAO, and to make it possible for the pilots of planes, where we permit them to fly over Canadian territory, to operate their radio sets. Obviously that is in the best interests of safe navigation by air. Similarly we take no exception to the idea that there should not be on the statute books legislation that denies to certain people, such as landed immigrants, the possibility of making their living by the driving of taxicabs which are equipped with two-way radio sets for the purpose of controlling their operations. If there are sections of this bill that are necessary to achieve those two purposes, then it seems to me to that extent to be quite in order and quite appropriate.
However, when one comes to this matter of making special provisions on a one-way basis for persons who are employed in Canada by the government of another country or any agency of the government of another country, I feel the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra (Mr. Green) was not stating it too strongly when he suggested that goes

a little too far. I have no objection to reciprocal arrangements with other countries, and that includes the United States. But it does seem to me that a provision for such reciprocal arrangements-in other words, for a privilege to be granted both ways-is already included in the Radio Act, section 7, subsection 4, paragraph (c). It says that:
The governor in council may, by regulation and on such terms and conditions as he may prescribe, exempt from the operation of this section a nonresident of Canada, who is a resident and citizen of a country that grants a reciprocal permission to Canadian citizens to be employed as radio operators in that country.
If the precise terms of that subsection do not go far enough I would have no objection to that subsection being amended, provided this whole arrangement is kept on a reciprocal basis. It seems to me that is the pith and substance of section 7, subsection 4, paragraph (c) as it now stands. Whatever is provided is on a reciprocal basis. On the other hand, the pith and substance as I see it of the corresponding part of the bill now before us is that we are asked to agree to persons from other countries working for the government of another country or the agency of government of another country in Canada having a special one-way privilege.
I have no desire to stir up any animosity towards any other country, friendly or otherwise; far from it. I see no particular point in trying to whip up any feeling with respect to national prestige or national pride, but it does seem to me it is a matter of common sense, and that it should be a matter of concern to us, that an arrangement like this be kept on a reciprocal basis. The minister indicated to us that the purpose of this part of the bill is to make a one-way arrangement of this kind with the United States, so that employees of the United States government or of an agency of the United States government might have a special privilege as radio operators in Canada. I believe that, particularly at this time in international affairs, when that country seems to be doing a lot of pushing around of other people and doing many things in an effort to get its own way, it would not hurt us to say to that country, this kind of arrangement is all right provided it is on a reciprocal basis. I hope the minister and the government, therefore, will, even at this late date in the stages of this piece of legislation, take another look at it and see if it is not possible to achieve what the minister and the government may feel has to be achieved on a reciprocal basis as provided in the act prior to the introduction of this bill, rather than on the one-way basis set out in Bill No. 446.
Radio Act
Perhaps the minister might let the matter stand in committee of the whole for this point to be considered or, since it does involve relations with other countries, he might be prepared to send the bill to the committee on external affairs. In any event, I hope that further consideration will be given by the minister to the point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, and the point to which I have spoken just now, namely that an arrangement of this kind should be kept on a reciprocal basis.

Now then, dealing with paragraph (b), and here I shall be limited to some extent in what I have to say because a great deal of this I cannot divulge to the house. I think that will explain the position to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. For instance, the Pine Tree stations in Canada are operated now by the United States government. Well, does anyone suggest that we should be operating radio stations in the United States? Well, the next group of stations are the United States air bases in Canada which were established prior to union with Newfoundland, some at Argentia, Fort Pepperrell, Harmon field, and I think there is one more, although I am not too sure. All of these stations are in operation now and they are being operated by radio operators who are not British subjects, under the powers contained in the order in council passed under the Emergency Powers Act. The same can be said of our own joint stations in the Arctic. By "these stations" I mean the joint weather stations operated by the Americans and the Canadians for meteorological services. There are, if my memory serves me right, some five such stations. There is one at Resolute, one at Isachsen, one at Mould Bay, one at Alert and the others leave my memory for the moment. These stations are operated jointly with the United States government, by virtue of an agreement which was made on the recommendation of the permanent joint board on defence. This was done as the order in council sets out, on the recommendation also of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). That is why paragraph (b) of the bill is placed therein. All paragraph (b) does is to carry into effect the powers taken under the Emergency Powers Act.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra raised the question of landed immigrants and suggested in his remarks that these should be limited to mobile stations. Let me say to him that a great deal, in fact the vast majority, of radio operations do not apply to mobile stations, but to permanent stations such as radiotelephony and radio operations in various locations which are permanent, in construction and tourist camps which are permanent and in a number of other stations. If an immigrant is not going to be allowed to be

Radio Act
exempt from the operations of that paragraph then many of these jobs cannot be taken by him.
Reference was made to subparagraph (ii) of paragraph (a) which reads:
holds a valid Canadian certificate of proficiency, or other authority to operate a radio station issued by the minister, or an equivalent certificate or authority issued by the country of which he is a citizen.
That is already in the act save the words underlined. Let me give an explanation of that and I think I can deal with the objection raised by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes).
The certificate of proficiency mentioned in the act is required in the more advanced and complicated type of radio communication such as the type my hon. friend had in mind: ship radio, ship-to-shore operation, airborne radio, such as a pilot who operates under the ICAO agreement over Canada. The pilot will not be allowed to operate radio unless there is evidence that he has met a requirement similar to that which we have here or something that is equal in standing. The proof of that is that we apply in our own country the requirement laid down by the international civil aviation organization.
Then, the certificate of proficiency has also to do with ground stations for communication with aircraft or with shipping. At the terminals all across Canada the terminals are in constant contact with the aircraft overhead going from one station to another and others are also in constant contact with shipping. Here we require a certificate of proficiency that has been approved by the department.
The same can be said of commercial communications where long distances are involved, but most other types of radio operating are dealt with by lesser authority which is not covered by a certificate such as that which I have been referring to. That has also been laid out in the radio regulations, and if any hon. member cares to obtain for himself these regulations he will find on page 6 regulation 13 (2). Perhaps I had better read regulation 13 (1) first and then (2), because they go together. Regulation 13 (1) reads as follows:
(1) No person shall act as a radio operator on any station in Canada without a Canadian certificate of proficiency in radio of such class as may be specified in the licence.
Now, this is the provision on which I wish to lay emphasis:
Nevertheless, the minister may at his discretion permit certain stations or classes of stations to be operated by persons who are not the holders of certificates of proficiency in radio, provided such persons are British subjects and capable of demonstrating to a departmental radio inspector that

they are proficient in the operation and maintenance of the equipment at the station on which they are employed.
Now, that section 13 paragraph (2) is designed to cover cases which are not at all like that raised by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich. It is designed to cover the case of the ordinary taxi driver who talks through a walkie-talkie with his office, and the case of the construction camp operator who is in control of a truck with a radio system operating from the truck to the office. However, the fact that he must be a British subject prohibits the landed immigrant from such employment. It seemed to us that it would only be fair and reasonable to allow that individual to operate this lesser class of radio station, if I may so call it that, so that if this bill is passed the regulation which I have just read would remain as it is to cover the secondary class, if it may be so called, and we would take out the words "provided such persons are British subjects"; thus in order to cover the landed immigrant the section would simply read:
Nevertheless, the minister may at his discretion permit certain stations or classes of stations to be operated by persons who are not the holders of certificates of proficiency in radio, provided such persons are capable of demonstrating to a departmental radio inspector that they are proficient in the operation and maintenance of the equipment at the station on which they are employed.
That would not affect in the slightest degree the complicated and more advanced kind of radio communications such as that employed by a pilot in an aircraft in which radio is essential, such as that operated by the mariner on the ship, or the experienced operator on shore who is in constant contact with the ship and equally, such as that used by the operator at an air terminal who is in constant contact with the pilot above.
As regards the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), I think he put his point extremely well because he stated that if only we would put into effect the explanatory notes then he could see no objection to this. Well, Mr. Speaker, that is exactly what was done in the (b) part and that, at least for the (b) part itself, is the object of this bill, the other part being there to clarify more than anything else. The object of the bill in part (b) is to carry into effect the provisions of the order in council, and I hope I have been successful in explaining to the house why it would not be practical to secure reciprocal arrangements for places such as those I described earlier.

order in council under the Emergency Powers Act. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLICING, HARBOUR TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to state now that at the conclusion of this debate a motion will be made to refer the bill to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, and therefore my opening remarks will tend to give as complete a picture as possible of the contemplated legislation whilst not burdening the house with lengthy details which can be obtained more efficiently when the measure is before the standing committee.
The National Harbours Board Act was passed by parliament in 1936. It has never been amended since that time, except in 1938, and that was to give the board power to sue and to be sued in its own name in tort. It is evident that over a period of some eighteen years many changes have occurred, and these amendments are being included for

National Harbours Board Act the purpose of bringing the act up to date. The purpose of these amendments is to clarify the existing legal position; to eliminate provisions which have been rendered superfluous by other acts; to remove cumbersome phrases and to make a few substantive alterations. While these are few in number, I should like to list them for the house now.
One has to do with the extension of the provisions of the act, to include additional persons who may be charged for services under the act. At the present time charges are made against owners. This amendment would extend the liability to include carriers and bailees as contrasted with the actual owners thereof. In many instances the carriers or the bailees are the only persons with whom the board has any dealings at all. Also to empower the governor in council to name a temporary member to the board where a member has been delegated to other governmental duties. This situation occurred during the second world war, and it was dealt with under the authority of the War Measures Act.
A new section is provided to eliminate all necessity of swearing in harbour police as special constables of some municipal or provincial police force or the R.C.M.P. The status created would be analogous to that established by the Railway Act for railway constables. To raise the limit of non-tender contracts from the former $10,000, fixed by the way in 1936, to $15,000; to empower the board on the approval of the governor in council to purchase and sell supplies, salvage and so forth; in fact, anything except land or real estate property up to a certain limit designated by the governor in council as the board's bylaws may prescribe. And here I wish to add that all the board's bylaws have to be approved by the governor in council.
There are also express provisions that the governor in council may make bylaws governing the handling, storing and so forth, even on private property in the board's harbours, of explosives or dangerous goods within any harbour under the board's jurisdiction.
There is also a section to enable the board to contract itself out of liability for negligence. In a number of instances, such as the granting of permission to bring explosives into a harbour, or the acceptance of highly perishable goods in storage, the revenue does not justify the risk incurred by the board unless the board, like any private operator in the same circumstances, possesses a capacity of restricting the liability which could conceivably arise through the negligence of some minor board employee.


There is also a clause in the bill to enable bylaws and the charges thereunder to be made binding on other agencies or departments of the crown, whether in the right of Canada or in that of any of the ten provinces, the reason being that the board operates to a large extent as a quasi-commercial corporation and must submit separate reports to parliament on its financial operation.
There is also an express provision in the bill for the acceptance by the courts of a copy of any bylaw, certified by the secretary of the board, as full evidence of such bylaw. This is merely a matter of convenience and is a common provision in statutes of this type.
There is also a clause to broaden the so-called "commutation authority" to cover explicitly commutations, reductions and waivers in respect of board charges imposed by bylaw.
There is a provision in the bill to give a general lien which would be enforceable against any goods of a debtor of the board whether or not the debt was incurred on the specific goods.
The period during which board tolls shall continue to accrue on goods seized and detained would be restricted to a maximum of thirty days. In the absence of such an amendment the period of accrual of charges could be almost unrestricted, and it is considered that this point should be clarified and explicitly covered.
There is an alteration extending the purview of the board's bylaws to all property under board administration as contrasted with the harbours alone. This would, for instance, apply to the grain elevators at Prescott and Port Colborne.
Apart from the foregoing, the bill also contains a few additional but very minor amendments which, like some of those already mentioned, effect no substantive change but serve to make more explicit, or to place in a more logical position within the act, provisions already existing. Such minor alterations would constitute a clarification of those provisions of the act relating to the awarding of contracts and relating to the use of harbours, and so forth, by vessels and aircraft; seizure, detention and sale of vessels and goods; board's right to sue for charges notwithstanding the seizure of goods and the repeal of a few obsolete provisions of the act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLICING, HARBOUR TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel something should be said on this bill by those who are concerned with the seaports of our eastern provinces because of the prominent part played in their life by

the national harbours board. Since the bill is to be referred to a committee for study I will make my remarks as brief as possible.
This is an act to amend the National Harbours Board Act and someone has said that it is routine with no great change in principle. While I would not go that far, Mr. Speaker, I think it might be suggested that it is an example of a government body grabbing more power, and it is an example of government by order in council.
There are one or two sections proposed in the bill which will fill the gap left by the Emergency Powers Act and the following considerations should be kept in mind when we consider the bill as a whole.
I believe most hon. members will agree that it is desirable we should have provision in our statute law for the efficient working of our waterfronts. In this regard we have two important matters that should be considered, and I refer to strikes and to explosions. It is necessary in this day and age that we have sufficient authority to deal with strikes, but we should be careful to consider the arbitrary power that might be given to police officers in dealing with such strikes.
The matter of explosions is also considered in this bill and I feel that in this respect we are still in need of greater restrictions as regards ammunition ships in our harbours. Surely the lessons of the Halifax explosion and others should convince us that we must be more careful in this respect. I think we are still behind the United States in the restrictions placed on ships in regard to explosives, and also in the authority given to the various boards that have to deal with such matters.
This bill has already been dealt with in the other place, and I feel it was given the most careful consideration by the other place both on second reading and when it went before the transport and communications committee. However there are still two or three points which bother me and I will just touch on them briefly now.
The matter of police officers and their policing duties is still a sore point. The bill deals with their appointment, jurisdiction, and authority, and while amendments were proposed in the other place which have cut down the further power sought by them I still feel an explanation will have to be given in committee as to some of their rights and powers. Their jurisdiction has been extended to cover a fifty-mile radius, and I would like an explanation, when the time comes, as to why such an extensive distance has been included.
National Harbours Board Act
Another matter which was referred to by the parliamentary assistant in his very careful explanation is the restriction on liability.
I feel that perhaps the right of the harbours board to be able to contract themselves out of certain liability as regards explosives responsibility in the various ports could be considered, though I feel that if this right is to be passed off to someone else there should be some restrictions on the parties who are to assume that right. In other words, we would not wish to see the responsibility for explosions in our harbours passed on to some bodies who are not in a position to accept this liability and to make amends in the case of an explosion.
Generally, I think the details of the bill are commendable. It is a good measure and we are pleased to see that the financial administration of the board is being changed in some respects so that it may come under the Financial Administration Act.
I believe that down our way the administration of the national harbours board has been fairly good, and I was pleased to see that new appointments were made at Ottawa the other day.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that this is another example of piecemeal legislation. In this legislation hunks have been taken out here and hunks thrown in there and it is rather confusing when one considers it all. But I would like to emphasize that we must be careful to bear the individual's rights in mind when considering this granting of arbitrary power to police officers. That, to my mind, is most important. The phrase "the rights of the individual" is used very loosely nowadays, and one can always argue these matters. Nevertheless when you get local conditions in which police officers of the harbours board come in contact with longshoremen and with men working in the ports there arises a considerable amount of animosity, though the actual criminal negligence that might be a consideration amounts only to petty pilfering, liquor traffic and things such as that. Therefore, we must strike the happy medium between the two, and we must see to it that the officers of the harbours board are given enough authority to conduct their business, though at the same time it must not be sufficiently arbitrary as to interfere with the rights of our citizens. We will be looking closely at this bill in committee.

I have read the bill through twice and I have found it very technical, so I am glad that the minister is going to refer the bill to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I find myself in the same position as the previous speaker in wishing to emphasize the importance of close and careful study being made of the bill when it is referred to that committee, and the fullest possible information being made available to members of the committee because I do not understand the technical aspects of this measure and I will certainly expect to hear some explanations when the committee meets.
As the hon. member who has just spoken pointed out, there is a change in the granting of authority for the appointment of police officers and I note that in their appointment these officers are to have the powers of peace officers within the meaning of the Criminal Code. That is quite understandable on property which is administered by the national harbours board, but I cannot understand why a special constable should have the authority of a peace officer, within the meaning of the Criminal Code, fifty miles away from the property owned or under the administration of the harbours board. It is because of these technical questions, which I feel should be explained, that I am very glad this bill is being referred to a committee of this house.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLICING, HARBOUR TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext: If the parliamentary assistant speaks now he will close the debate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLICING, HARBOUR TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my appreciation of the reasonable tone adopted by the two hon. members who spoke on this subject here tonight. I wish to refer briefly to some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell). I can assure him that it is not the purpose of the bill to grab more power, as he expressed it, but rather that it is brought forward, as I said in my opening statement, only to clarify the existing act and to add whatever modifications or amendments have proved themselves to be necessary over a period of some eighteen years of experience and operation by the national harbours board.
He made some reference to regulations with regard to explosives. There are in force comprehensive regulations made under the authority of the Canada Shipping Act. There are also some regulations made by the national harbours board and also some under the authority of the Railway Act. But with regard to the carrying of explosives in naval


vessels, may I say that this matter comes under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) exclusively.
Both the hon. member for Saint John-Albert and the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) have expressed some views with regard to the making of harbour constables into peace officers and have also expressed some opposition to their jurisdiction over a distance of fifty miles, as mentioned in the bill. I must repeat here that all we propose to do is to give the harbour constables a status which is comparable to that at present enjoyed by railway constables under the Railway Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLICING, HARBOUR TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask the parliamentary assistant a question on that point?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLICING, HARBOUR TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLICING, HARBOUR TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext: Is it not a fact that under the Railway Act the jurisdiction is only half a mile?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLICING, HARBOUR TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext:
No. I wish to refer my hon. friend here to section 456 of the Railway Act and subsequent sections, especially section 457 which gives the territorial limits of constables' jurisdiction as follows:
Every constable so appointed, who has taken such or made such declaration, may act as a constable for the preservation of the peace, and for the security of persons and property against unlawful acts
(a)	on such railway, and on any of the works belonging thereto;
(b)	on and about any trains, roads, wharfs, quays, landing places, warehouses, lands and premises belonging to such company, whether the same are in the county, city, town, parish, district or other local jurisdiction within which he was appointed or in any other place through which such railway passes or in which the same terminates, or through or to which any railway passes which is worked or leased by such company; and
(c)	in all places not more than a quarter of a mile distant from such railway.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLICING, HARBOUR TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext: It is a quarter of a mile. I said half a mile.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLICING, HARBOUR TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext: It might be more than a quarter of a mile from the place where the offence was committed-it is a quarter of a mile from the railway, but it extends over the distance which the railway runs.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLICING, HARBOUR TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext: There is a big difference between that and fifty miles.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLICING, HARBOUR TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext:
To answer this point about the fifty-mile territorial jurisdiction of a constable of the national harbours board I must say, for example, that the harbour of Montreal extends over a distance of some thirty miles and, if my memory serves me correctly, it is in four different municipal

districts. The same thing applies to the harbour at Vancouver. The hon. member for Vancouver East will correct me if I am wrong, but I think the property of the national harbours board in the port of Vancouver extends over the districts of three different municipalities, namely that of Vancouver city, that of Burnaby and that of North Vancouver. That is why it has been found necessary to give this fifty-mile territorial limit to the jurisdiction of harbours board constables.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLICING, HARBOUR TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask the parliamentary assistant a question on that point?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLICING, HARBOUR TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLICING, HARBOUR TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext: Is it not a fact that the bill gives these constables jurisdiction over all the harbours board property and, in addition, over fifty miles in every direction from the harbours board property?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING POLICING, HARBOUR TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext:
I must remind my hon. friend that the offence must have been committed in connection with some of the board's property and the fifty-mile limit- and this will be explained in much more detail when the bill is before the standing committee-is, as I understand it, from the property in connection with which the offence was committed. I must give another instance. For example, suppose you have a motorist violating the speed limit on the Jacques Cartier bridge in Montreal. It is rather difficult to determine exactly where the offence was committed. Was it committed just on that line separating the two municipalities of Montreal on this side and St. Lambert, I think it is, on the other side? In addition to that consideration, you must give the board's constable the right to pursue this violator of the speed limit, and he may have to travel quite a few miles chasing the motorist. In any event, as I stated, many more instances and reasons in support of this particular feature of the bill will be given when it is before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I just wish to say that, before this standing committee, every opportunity will be given to hon. members to get any information they wish from the representatives of the national harbours [DOT]board and their counsel, who will be in attendance.
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) I move that this bill be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
