subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure respecting allowances for disabled persons and to provide for the payment to the provinces out of the consolidated revenue fund of amounts in respect of allowances for disabled persons paid by the provinces, to certain persons who have attained the age of eighteen years, and who are totally and permanently disabled and in need of such allowances, not exceeding in respect of any recipient fifty per centum of forty dollars monthly or of the amount of the allowance paid by the provinces monthly to the recipients, whichever is the lesser; and to provide for the making of agreements with the provinces in relation thereto and for the conditions and duration of such agreements.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Is the minister going to make a brief statement about the matter at this
stage?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I had thought that if we could agree to have the discussion of the measure on second reading it might avoid duplication and save some time. Of course I am in the hands of the committee.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
I think it will meet with the approval of hon. members generally that we have the main discussion of this legislation on second reading and in committee of the whole. May I take a minute or two to suggest to the minister that in view of such information as is contained in the resolution now before us I hope he will come prepared at these other stages to deal rather seriously with certain points. I shall refrain from going into them in any detail at this time, but I do wish to suggest that as the resolution now reads it indicates certain inadequacies in the proposed legislation.
The house has been asking for legislation of this kind and waiting for it for a long time, and I do hope that when it is brought in the definition of "disabled"-with those qualifying words "totally and permanently" -will not be so restrictive as to limit the pension to too few of those of our citizens

Disabled Persons-Allowances who need and deserve it. I also want to say that when we reach the later stages we will have something to say about the proposed amount, the age at which it is to be paid, the fifty-tifty division between Ottawa and the provinces, the residence qualification, the means test and other matters. In other words, as the minister knows we welcome this legislation but there is certainly room for improvement in the terms in which it is forecast and we hope that those improvements may be made even before the bill is introduced.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Last year when a similar resolution presented by a private member was before the house I think every hon. member was in favour of it. It is a matter that has been before the house a great many times during the past few years. We welcome this resolution. We are glad that the legislation is being introduced, and we also feel that we would like to withhold our comments until the bill is up for second reading. This is not going to be an easy bill. I quite realize, and I pointed out to the house last year, the difficulties in trying to formulate some type of legislation to cover the proof of disability. At that time I cited the various regulations in vogue in the United States where a bill of this type was brought before the legislative body some years ago. Practically every state to which I referred gives a different meaning to total and permanent disability.
When the matter was before the house last year I remember describing it as a gap in our social security program. Therefore I appreciate the fact that the bill is now being brought in, and we will discuss it clause by clause when it comes up later.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister a question. He mentioned previously in the house that certain provinces had not passed enabling legislation and others had. I wonder whether he intends to give us that information this evening. Perhaps the Secretary of State can also help us out in this regard. I see him helping the minister. I know that this legislation is being anticipated with a great deal of hope and expectation by people throughout Canada. I have in mind particularly a young couple in my own constituency with four children, three of whom are totally and permanently disabled. This kind of thing is a tragedy. It is a terrific handicap not only to the parents but to the child who is well. I hope that the legislation will cover them. I should also like to know whether or not the enabling legislation in the various provinces will in any way hinder the coming into operation of the act.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext: Would the minister make a statement with respect to the enabling legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext: I had suggested to the house that perhaps this was not the moment for a general discussion of the measure. Having expressed that wish I would not want to violate what I urged on the committee. Therefore I will simply say that when the measure does reach second reading I will be prepared to discuss it in detail and to indicate that the bill in its main features was discussed with all the provincial governments. Generally speaking it represents not a compromise but an acceptance of their most common position, and I am sure when the measure is introduced it will appeal to all hon. members as a very important contribution toward providing assistance to a great segment of our population whom we all, within our capacity, want to help.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext: We can all agree with that, but the point as to whether or not certain provinces have passed enabling legislation is not something that you are going to put in or leave out of the legislation. I wanted to get the information. After the very fine discussions the minister has had with the provinces, perhaps he might tell us how many of them have already passed enabling legislation. Could he not give the committee that information now?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Some five provinces have already passed enabling legislation. While I am on my feet, I should like to say at the outset to the house and to the country that, while I am sponsoring the bill, the real author of the legislation is the Prime Minister himself. Within a week of the holding of the last general election the Prime Minister wrote to me from his summer home. He said that he had been giving this matter his attention and he was now of the opinion, although the matter had not been discussed in the months immediately before the election, that this was a measure to which we should now address ourselves. I think that I should pay this tribute to the Prime Minister's humanitarian instincts by saying that this bill would not have been introduced at this time but for the initiative which he himself took.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.
Mr. Martin thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 462, to provide for allowances for disabled persons.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LICENCES, REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Before anything is said on this matter, I want to rise on a question of privilege. It is now past ten o'clock, our adjournment time. If we are to continue each evening for some further period then there should be a motion moved in the house to make the procedure regular. I know there are some members who would prefer, if the working day is going to be lengthened, that we should lengthen it in the morning rather than at night. There may be others who are of a different mind, but the house should decide and we should not be carrying on without a vote of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LICENCES, REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, it is the government's intention, based I understand on the unanimous consent of other parties in the house, to present a motion that commencing next Monday morning we shall sit in the mornings. In the meantime, however, if the house feels that they can do extra work for an hour in the evening, I think perhaps that ought to be done if it suits hon. members. Rather than make a formal motion to cover the whole of the time, we thought that perhaps each evening a decision might be made, having in mind the amount of work done and the general progress made.
If that is not acceptable we could, of course, make a formal motion, but I suggest that we should not. Each evening at ten o'clock, if hon. members feel they can carry on for another hour they might do so, for the time being at least, and for tonight I suggest we might carry on until eleven and consider the situation tomorrow.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LICENCES, REGULATIONS, ETC.

Opium and Narcotic Drug Act and therefore I would not want to impose upon him now the order for the rest of the week if that did not suit him.
